Bullet Journaling 101 — A Guide for Complete Beginners
Phoenix Smith
Follow
4 min read
·
Nov 7, 2025

Hello everyone! It was really hard for me to get started with bullet journaling, so this week’s post is all about how to do that. A quick note — a lot of this is just suggestions, so don’t take anything word for word. This guide is meant to be just that — a guide. Not a dictator.

Don’t Rush

The biggest mistake I made when first starting out was rushing into it. But bullet journaling costs money and time — two valuable things no one wants to waste. You can’t do it in one day. So stop hunting for supplies and grab yourself a piece of blank paper. It’s time to plan.

The Planning Process

I’m hoping to one day post a step-by-step for a more detailed bullet journal planning process, but since this is for beginners, I’ll waterdown my usual process into three steps; supplies, theme, and layout.

Supplies

Before you fill up your Amazon cart, you need to think about what you’re buying. There are really only two essential things you need (a notebook and pen), but many people grab additional stationary. I’ll only be going over the necessities here.

Notebooks

First things first — a notebook.

You can’t start painting without a canvas, so the first thing you’ll need to get is a notebook. There are four things you need to look at when buying a notebook; type, paper, size and format. I’ll go over each one in more detail.

Type

There are four main notebook types; hardcover, softcover, composition, and spiral. Hardcover works best in the long run, but spiral notebooks allow more flexibility for where you place your notebook (which is useful if you’re wanting to make your spreads and pages look pretty). I personally look for a notebook that has both of these qualities, but prefer long-lasting hardcovers over spiral notebooks.

Paper

Paper is one of the biggest aspects to look at. Higher-quality paper reduces bleed (my nemesis), but can be more expensive. How do you determine quality, you ask? GSM. GSM stands for grams per square meter, and basically represents how thick the paper is. The higher the GSM, the less likely it is to bleed.

Size

When picking a notebook, you need to know how big you want it to be. Smaller sizes are more portable, but have less space to write. Larger sizes are better for detailed use, but can be a pain to carry around. You need to find a good balance that fits you. The main notebook sizes are A4, A5, A6, and pocket-sized. I recommend A5, as it’s a good balance between available space and portability.

Format

There are several aspects to formatting, the big ones being ruling and spacing. Ruling refers to the design on the page — do you want a classic lined notebook that provides structure, or blank pages for more flexibility? I suggest getting a notebook with some kind of grid ruling (I personally prefer dot ruling), as it provides a good middle ground between structure and flexibility.

Spacing is how far apart any present lines are from each other. This is commonly measured in millimeters (mm). If you’re getting lined paper, you’ll typically want more spacing than if you wanted grid paper. And if you are more interested in grid paper, I’d suggest around 5mm spacing. (Fun fact: that’s close to the width of a highlighter nib!)

Pens

The next bit of supplies you need to worry about is pens. Gel pens are more common due to their versatility, but regular ballpoint works well too. Gel pens also come in thousands of different colors, so be sure to pick a set that has what you want.

Theme

Now that you have your supplies picked out, it’s time to pick a theme. This step is completely optional, but I highly recommend it. A set theme helps your notebook feel unique, and can guide your creativity. But a good theme is planned, so don’t go picking one randomly. Pick something that you like and feel like you have the energy for. I suggest a simpler theme for your first journals, but ambition can be an unstoppable force some times.

Layout

Bullet journals are made up of two things — spreads and pages (Spreads refers to a set of two side-by-side pages). It’s a good idea to plan out what you want to have in your bullet journal before getting started. If you need inspiration or ideas, I suggest going to Pinterest and looking some up. Pinterest is a great resource for bullet journaling inspiration, and there’s so many different ideas it can give you. You don’t even need an account to browse (You do need one to save ideas for later, but screenshotting is also an option if you don’t mind swamping your gallery).

I hope that was helpful, and I hope you find bullet journaling a great tool for your productivity, mental health, and/or organization.
